editions.text:
September 13 closed with 142 feeder visits and 15 species, a marked increase from the previous week’s average of 50.5 visits and 9.2 species. The station’s first confident visual records of a Gray Catbird and a House Finch occurred during this busy period, with the House Finch perched on the top ring of the black metal feeder stand. Tufted Titmice dominated the visual counts with 75 sightings, while Northern Cardinals and Carolina Chickadees provided the primary acoustic activity.

The high traffic aligns with the installation of a new tube seed feeder and the replacement of the old seed feeder at 16:04 to resolve detection issues. These changes occurred alongside the switch to the pi-mic audio source at 06:52, which facilitated the first-time ear detections of Carolina Chickadees, House Finches, Northern Mockingbirds, and Ruby-throated Hummingbirds. Regulars such as Carolina Wrens, Eastern Towhees, and American Crows maintained their consistent presence throughout the day.

Tufted Titmice remained active from just before sunrise until shortly before sunset.

A hummingbird was first on the station, arriving just thirteen minutes after sunrise before a Blue Jay followed ten minutes later. By 07:42, the Carolina Wren had begun its persistent vocalizations, establishing the morning's acoustic baseline with three detections before the first feeder visit.

Traffic surged rapidly through the second hour, with Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees becoming the visual mainstays of the feeders. A Red-shouldered Hawk called from the canopy, its presence noted alongside the rising volume of Carolina Wren song that dominated the 08:00 hour.

By 10:30, the station had logged 163 visits and 15 species, significantly outpacing the recent average of 39 visits at this time.

The afternoon has held steady under a high of 28.0 degrees, with wind barely moving at 3 kph. The station has logged 228 visits so far, a figure far above the recent average of 52.1 at this time. Tufted Titmice remain the visual mainstay with 94 confident sightings, while Carolina Chickadees contribute the bulk of the remaining traffic with 67 visits.

Acoustic activity has continued to build, with Carolina Wrens accounting for 121 detections, far exceeding any other species. Blue Jays have become more prominent in the midday hours, registering 32 heard and 3 visual visits, alongside a single American Crow. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird was last confirmed at the station in the morning, with 11 probable visits total.

The day's traffic is consistent with the recent upward trend, following yesterday's 142 visits. The station has seen 15 species so far, matching the recent high but well above the weekly average of 9.4.

The day concluded with 244 feeder visits, nearly four times the recent average of 63.6. In the final hours, the midday noise retreated, leaving only the persistent vocalizations of Carolina Wrens and Northern Cardinals. A single Black-crowned Night Heron was detected in the 20:00 hour, a species not typically on the regional list for this time of year. This detection stands apart from the station's usual chorus, which was dominated by 129 Carolina Wren detections and the visual presence of 96 Tufted Titmice. The final visual record of the day was a Ruby-throated Hummingbird at sunset, bringing the total confirmed sightings to 14.
